# Notes on Jeremiah 43

**A note on what I found.** Most of these notes come from the older commentaries on biblehub, studylight and blueletterbible, and from Enduring Word. I didn't find pages on this chapter from the sites for each Protestant tradition (Ligonier, Desiring God, wesley.nnu.edu, LCMS and so on), or from netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org or oca.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so that section is left out.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Poole points out that the text says twice that Jeremiah spoke only what the Lord sent him to say. He takes this as a model: preachers should pass on only what they have received from the Lord, even if they put it in their own words. The prophet is very exact in letting us know that he had from the Lord what he delivered to them, he therefore twice repeats it — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm

**v. 2:**
- Poole says the men are called "proud" partly because of their rank. Mainly, though, it is because they trusted their own judgment more than the prophet's guidance. He calls that kind of pride a root of disobedience. Saying outright that they knew better than God would have been atheism, so instead they denied that God had sent Jeremiah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm
- Matthew Henry thinks they probably knew the message was from God but would not admit it. His lesson: people deny Scripture is God's word because they have already decided not to obey it. Either they were not convinced that what was said came from God or (which I rather think) though they were convinced of it they would not own it. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm
- Guzik notes that these men had lived through every one of Jeremiah's prophecies coming true. They said this *despite* the evidence, not because of the evidence. He also quotes Kidner: they had treated God as a power to recruit rather than a Lord to obey. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/

**v. 3:**
- Guzik calls the charge against Baruch ridiculous. He quotes Feinberg: a prophet who wouldn't soften his message for a king would hardly be steered by his secretary. He also quotes Cundall, who says it isn't clear what Baruch could have gained. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- Poole agrees that a clerk was unlikely to push the prophet into betraying his people. Henry says that people who refuse to give up their sin paint those who warn them as schemers, and that the wrongly accused can take comfort that their witness is in heaven. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm

**v. 4:** Guzik: in 42:5–6 the people promised to do whatever God said. God told them to stay in the land, and they broke that promise and went to Egypt for safety and supplies. He quotes Cundall: Egypt, the "arm of flesh," seemed safer to them than the arm of the Lord. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/

**vv. 5–6:**
- Poole says Jeremiah, Baruch and probably many of the people did not want to go. The captains forced them, so that many became a kind of prisoners to their own countrymen. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm
- Guzik sees Jeremiah and Baruch as hostages held against God. God had threatened judgment on everyone who went to Egypt (42:17), so the leaders were in effect daring Him to punish His own prophet. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- On "the king's daughters," Clarke is surprised the Babylonians left any of the royal family. He suggests they may not have known about them, or thought them unable to inherit because they were daughters of concubines or because they were women. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jeremiah/43.htm
- Henry suggests the leaders brought the prophets along so it would look as if the prophets had come willingly. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm

**v. 7:**
- Clarke: the Greeks called Tahpanhes Daphne. He thinks the group probably stopped there to get Pharaoh's permission to go further into Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jeremiah/43.htm
- Poole thinks the city may have been named after Queen Tahpenes (1 Kings 11:19). He reads verse 9 as showing that Pharaoh lived or kept a palace there. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: God had freed Abraham's descendants from Egypt, and nearly 900 years later they went back as a defeated remnant. Chuck Smith sees Egypt as a picture of the life of sin, and says the people went back out of fear and lack of faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/jeremiah-43.html
- The Bible Hub study page connects this with Deuteronomy 17:16 and Isaiah 31:1. It says going back to Egypt meant reversing their salvation, trusting human power and taking on idolatry. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/43.htm

**v. 8:**
- Guzik: Jeremiah was taken by force, so God did not count him as disobedient, and he was still God's prophet. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: the people had not escaped God or got beyond the reach of His word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- Henry: the word of the Lord is not bound, prophecy was not limited to Israel's land, and God did not withdraw His favour from a prophet who went to Egypt under force. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm

**v. 9:**
- **What kind of act it was.** Ellicott groups it with Jeremiah's other acted-out signs: the broken pot (ch. 19) and the yoke (ch. 27). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- **Who watched.** Henry: the act was done for the people of Judah, not the Egyptians. Jeremiah couldn't stop them going, but he might bring them to repent of it. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm
- **"Brick-kiln" or "pavement."** Commentators disagree about the word:
  - Ellicott prefers "mortar on the platform" and thinks a brick-kiln at a palace door seems out of place. — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/43-9.htm
  - Barnes suggests a brick pavement. He thinks Jeremiah built a small model of a royal dais and plastered it over. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
  - JFB thinks the palace was being built or repaired, which explains the mortar. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
  - Gill thinks it was a place where bricks were shaped, by a gate of the palace grounds rather than the main entrance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-9.html
  - Calvin takes it as a kiln or brick-making place near the palace gate. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-9.html
- **What the materials mean.** Keil & Delitzsch: Pharaoh's palace was brick, while Babylon's throne would stand on large stones. The materials picture how strong and lasting each kingdom is. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- **The Exodus echo.** Henry says Egypt's ruin was founded in "that clay." The Biblical Illustrator says the brick-kiln would remind them of their ancestors' forced labour. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/sermons/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- **Was it allowed?** The Pulpit Commentary, quoting Streane, says Jeremiah was protected: those who accepted him saw him as a prophet, and others took him for insane, which in Eastern eyes meant divinely prompted. The stones would later testify that he had predicted the events. — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- **Location.** Guzik quotes Thompson: Jeremiah probably buried the stones some way from the building, since a refugee would hardly be allowed to dig up a finished pavement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/

**v. 10:**
- **"My servant."** Henry: God calls Nebuchadnezzar His servant because the king carried out God's will. Poole: he obeyed God though he intended not so. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm
- **Why such a small detail.** Henry: it was foretold so that when it happened, people would remember the prophecy and be sure that God knows even the smallest events in advance. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm
- **The stones and the canopy.** Guzik quotes Thompson: the stones stood for a base for Nebuchadnezzar's throne. The word for "royal pavilion" (or canopy) appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- Bible.org's note lists possible meanings for that word: pavilion, canopy, carpet, or sceptre. — https://bible.org/book/export/html/21217

**v. 11:**
- Henry: the Jews brought the Babylonians into Egypt after them. Those who promised to protect Israel from the king of Babylon exposed themselves to him. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm
- Guzik: the Babylonian army would bring death, captivity and the sword. If the refugees ran to Egypt to escape Babylon, Babylon would follow them there. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- Barnes is quoted as saying God makes one wicked nation a scourge to another. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-13.htm

**v. 12:**
- **Burning the gods.** Clarke: wooden idols would be burned and metal ones, some of gold, carried away. Gill reads it the same way. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-43.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-12.htm
- **"As a shepherd wraps himself in his garment."** Most older writers read this as ease:
  - Clarke: done with ease, little resistance, and confidence that it is now his. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jeremiah/43.htm
  - Barnes: as easily as a shepherd throws on his cloak for a night in the field. JFB: as a shepherd puts on his cloak before moving his flock. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-12.htm
  - Poole: the soldiers will go home dressed in Egypt's better clothing. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-12.htm
  - Henry: he will wear Egypt's spoils as both ornament and armour. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-12.html
  - Calvin: "roll up," the way a shepherd gathers his things to move on. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-12.html
- **"Depart in peace."** The Bible Hub study note says this underlines how certain the prophecy is. — https://biblehub.com/study/jeremiah/43-12.htm

**v. 13:**
- Beth-shemesh means "house of the sun." JFB identifies it with the city the Greeks called Heliopolis and Genesis 41:45 calls On. Barnes says the "images" were really pillars or obelisks, and Heliopolis was famous for them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-13.htm
- Pulpit identifies them as the obelisks of the temple of Ra, the sun god. — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/43-13.htm
- Henry finds it striking that Nebuchadnezzar, an idolater who also honoured the sun, is the one used to destroy Egypt's idols. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_043.cfm
- Poole says the passage shows that pagans gave divine worship to created things. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/43.htm
- **Fulfilment.**
  - Guzik quotes Harrison: an inscription records Nebuchadnezzar invading Egypt in 568/567 BC, more as a punishing raid than a full conquest. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
  - JFB cites Josephus for a campaign in the fifth year after Jerusalem fell. It also mentions an Arab-reported tradition that Egypt was laid waste because its king had sheltered the Jews. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-13.htm
  - The ISBE article says the prophecy was fulfilled "at least in its general sense." — https://studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/isb/t/tahpanhes.html

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no real disagreement between traditions on this chapter. The writers I read come from several backgrounds:
- Calvin (Reformed)
- Henry and Poole (Puritan)
- Gill (Baptist)
- Clarke (Methodist)
- Guzik and Chuck Smith (charismatic-leaning evangelical)

They all read it the same way: a warning against rejecting God's word and trusting human help, God still speaking to His prophet in Egypt, and the sign foretelling Babylon's invasion. Where they differ (kiln or pavement in v. 9, what the garment picture means in v. 12), it is over wording, not doctrine.

---

## 3. Other views

**v. 9: the Hebrew text.**
- The Cambridge Bible calls the Hebrew text questionable here. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has only "in the fore-court." Another ancient reading has "in secret," which leads some scholars to think the act took place at night. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- The Latin Vulgate has "in the crypt which is under the brick walls." — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/43-9.htm

**v. 9: archaeology (the sources conflict).**
- Several sources link the spot to a brick pavement that Flinders Petrie dug up at Tell Defenneh: Harrison (quoted by Guzik), and the Cambridge Bible, which dates it to Psammetichus I and the 1886 dig. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-9.htm
- Chuck Smith goes further. He says Petrie found the very stones Jeremiah buried, places the dig in the 1920s, and says the stones are in a Cairo museum. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-9.html
- The other sources claim only that the platform may be the place, not that the stones were found. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-43.html

**v. 12: "lice" instead of "garment."**
- NIV, ESV, NET, NRSV and NAB translate it as a shepherd picking his cloak clean of lice. — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/43-12.htm
- The Cambridge Bible prefers this reading, which follows the Greek Old Testament: wrecking Egypt will be as easy as picking vermin off a cloak. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/43-12.htm
- Constable says it is possibly what Jeremiah meant. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-12.html
- Coffman disagrees strongly. He calls the Good News Bible's version a "preposterous mistranslation" and sides with Keil, who calls other explanations "lexically untenable." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/43-12.html

**vv. 6–7: how Jeremiah died (Catholic and other traditions).**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia reports a tradition, first found in Tertullian, that Jeremiah's own countrymen stoned him in Egypt for his warnings. It links this to Hebrews 11:37 and says Jeremias would not have died as Jeremias had he not died a martyr. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08334a.htm
- Catholic Answers says he probably died at Tahpanhes, stoned by the same men. It also presents him as a figure of Christ. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/jeremiah
- Clarke (quoted by Guzik) gives Jerome as the source for the stoning at Tahpanhes. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-43/
- Got Questions notes that Scripture doesn't record his death, and mentions a different Jewish tradition: Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon, where he died. — https://www.gotquestions.org/how-did-Jeremiah-die.html

**v. 9: reading the stones as pointing to Christ.**
- One Bible Hub article sees the buried stones as foreshadowing the "cornerstone" passages applied to the Messiah (Psalm 118:22, 1 Peter 2:6). — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_are_stones_important_in_Jer_43_9.htm
- The chapter study page calls Jeremiah a type of Christ, rejected by his own people. This is devotional application, not a mainstream reading of the verse. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/43.htm
